## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Upāhanajātaka* (Ja 231), also titled *Upāhanajātakam* and translated in modern scholarship as "A Pair of Sandals", is a canonical story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at the Veḷuvana monastery (the Bamboo Grove) and relates to the Buddha's schismatic disciple Devadatta [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. While assembled in the Hall of Truth (*dhammasabhā*), the monks discuss how Devadatta repudiated his teacher (*ācariya*), became an adversary of the Tathāgata, and suffered utter ruin [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. Entering the hall, the Buddha states that Devadatta had likewise repudiated his teacher and come to destruction in a previous existence, and he proceeds to recount a story of the past [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].

In the tale of the past (*atītavatthu*), an ungrateful pupil (*dutthantevāsika*) turns on his teacher and is killed after foolishly rivaling him [Fausböll 1879]. Approaching the king, the Bodhisatta delivers two verses (*gāthādvayam*) based on the metaphor of footwear: just as a pair of shoes bought for personal comfort causes injury and bites the wearer's feet when heated by the sun and pressed against the sole, so too learning or craft (*sippa*) acquired by an unworthy person brings about his own destruction [Fausböll 1879]. The king bestows great honor upon the Bodhisatta, and in the story's identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that the pupil was Devadatta and the teacher was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1879].

SuttaCentral records four translations of the Jātaka in four modern languages [SuttaCentral]. Machine text-reuse matching by DharmaNexus indicates five passages shared between the text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Atk S0513a2), with the longest match covering verses §1.1–2.4 and commentary sections §1423–1427 [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus records any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan literature [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
